CITATION
:

Warman
v.
National Post Company
, 2015 ONSC 267

COURT
FILE:
08-CV-00352197SR

MOTION
HEARD:
20140514

RELEASED:

20150126

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE – ONTARIO

RE:

RICHARD WARMAN

Plaintiff

v.

THE NATIONAL POST COMPANY, JONATHAN
KAY, EZRA LEVANT, KATHY SHAIDLE, FIVEFEETOFFURY.COM, SMALLDEADANIMALS.COM,
CATHERINE MCMILLAN, MARK FOURNIER, FREEDOMINION.CA, CONSTANCE
WILKINS-FOURNIER

Defendants

BEFORE:
MASTER D. E. SHORT

COUNSEL:

Peter Jacobsen
and Julia Lefebvre                fax: 416-982-3801

Counsel for the Defendant

Ezra
Levant (Moving Party)

Brian Shiller and Angela Chaisson                fax:
416-964-8305

Counsel
for the Plaintiff

Richard Warman

RELEASED:  January 26, 2015

Reasons for Decision

I.          Background

[
1
]

This action was commenced in 2008 and continues
as a Simplified Procedure matter in accord with Rule 76 of the
Rules of
Civil Procedure
. That rule was amended after this action was commenced to
entitle each party to a two hour Examination for Discovery of the party
opposite. These are the third set of reasons I have delivered in this dispute.
The parties still have not conducted discoveries and continue to argue matters
in the production phase of this litigation.

[
2
]

This action involves a claim in defamation for various
internet postings published by the Defendants, including allegations that the
Plaintiff is the author of racist postings on various websites, and that the
Plaintiff used false names, or "personas" to communicate with
individuals and make these postings.

[
3
]

I am advised that Mr. Warman has filed over 26
complaints under s. 13 of the Canadian Human Rights Act (the "CHRA")
complaining of "hate speech", mostly published on websites. He has
admitted to using "false personas" on these web sites, posing as a
racist and writing racist posts, in order to invite a response from other
readers of the site. He would then bring a Section 13 complaint based in part
on the response to his postings.

[
4
]

Mr. Levant (the Defendant”) takes issue with the
manner in which Mr. Warman has undertaken these prosecutions, and in
particular, asserted that Mr. Warman made a particularly odious Internet
posting with respect to a respected Canadian woman. Mr. Warman denies that he
was responsible for that publication (referred to in my reasons as the “Hateful
Posting”) and seeks damages for defamation and an apology.

[
5
]

The hateful posting appeared to come from a
specific IP address, which has been established as being the IP address of the Plaintiff’s
computer.

[
6
]

The Defendant brought a motion before me in
March 2010 seeking an examination of the Plaintiffs computer (the "Warman
Laptop") by an independent computer expert and the production of a report
on the examination.

[
7
]

In my first reasons in this matter I expressed my
view that the, then newly enacted, concept of “proportionality” was a virtue to
be sought after in Ontario’s justice system. I regret that this case has identified
some of the major challenges to the successful implementation of a concept that
was intended to make for a more economical, expeditious and efficient approach
to dispute resolution .

II.        The Issue in the Action

[
8
]

The motions to date have thus focused on the
appropriate degree of access to Mr. Warman’s computer hard drive by way of
documentary discovery.

[
9
]

My initial lengthy judgment in this matter was
released on August 16, 2010. The detailed facts surrounding the dispute are set
out in those reasons found at
Warman v. National Post Co.,

2010 ONSC
3670
; 103 O.R. (3d) 174; 77 C.C.L.T. (3d) 122;
2010 CarswellOnt 5920
.

[
10
]

An Addendum which , in part gives rise to these
reasons can be found at
Warman v. National Post Co.,
103 O.R. (3d) 423
;

2010 ONSC 5828
.That
Addendum
read in part:

[2] Since the release of [the first]
decision, counsel for the main protagonists have been attempting to achieve a
mutually acceptable approach to the examination of the subject hard-drive in
what I agree is "somewhat uncharted territory".

[3] I have reviewed their proposed
approach to addressing potential issues of privilege claims arising with
respect to the data on the drive and find that it seems a practical approach in
this case.

[4] Having regard to the possible
utility of this approach in other cases, I have formally issued this addendum
on consent.

[
11
]

I therefore established a protocol with respect
to the examination of the contents of the subject hard drive by a mutually
acceptable, neutral individual who would serve as the Independent Computer
Expert (“ICE”).

[
12
]

The parties negotiated at length with respect to
the proposed terms of the governing document, and ultimately, I established
what was referred to as the ICE Privilege Protocol. The relevant provisions read:

“1.        The ICE shall provide Mr.
Shiller on behalf of his client ("the plaintiff") with his final
report ("the Report") and at the same time advises Peter Jacobsen on
behalf of his client ("the defendant") that he has done so.

2.         The plaintiff must
determine whether he asserts solicitor-client privilege over any of the
material that the ICE has included in the Report, within 20 days of the
plaintiff receiving the Report ("within the 20 days").

3.         If there is any
information contained in the Report over which the plaintiff asserts
solicitor-client privilege, the plaintiff is to, within the 20 days:

i.

identify such with full particularity in a
Schedule "B" to an Affidavit of Documents and;

ii.

provide the defendant with an appropriately
redacted version of the Report which will have as redactions only that
information which the plaintiff has listed in his Schedule "B" list
and the Schedule "B" to an Affidavit of Documents.

4.         The plaintiff is to
maintain the Report, i.e.: the original unredacted expert's report, and file
it, sealed with the court, in the event that the defendant brings any challenge
to the plaintiff's assertion of solicitor-client privilege so that the court
can see what has been redacted by the plaintiff.”

III.       The Parties and the Present
Dispute

[
13
]

Mr. Warman is a human rights lawyer who has
monitored the activities of the white supremacist and neo-Nazi movements for
the past 20 years. Over the preceding 12 years he has drafted, filed, and successfully
co-litigated 16 complaints under the Internet hate messaging provision of the
Canadian Human Rights Act.  Mr. Warman has been honoured for his work by the
Law Society of Upper Canada, the B’nai Brith League for Human Rights, the
Canadian Jewish Congress, and was awarded the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Medal.

[
14
]

The Defendant Ezra Levant is a well-known
Canadian journalist and television personality who published allegations with
respect to the conduct of the Plaintiff and the Hateful Posting.

[
15
]

The factum submitted by Mr. Warman’s counsel
asserts:

“As a result of his human rights
work, Mr. Warman has endured extensive efforts by white supremacists and
neo-Nazis at retaliation including repeated death threats and virtually
anything else that they can think up including using the Internet to defame him
and attempt to undermine his credibility.  The unfounded allegation that Mr.
Warman authored the Hateful Posting was one such attack.”

[
16
]

On October 25, 2010, I ordered that an
independent computer expert (“ICE”) examine a mirror image of Mr. Warman’s hard
drive. The ICE Report was to address a very narrow issue: does any evidence
exist that Mr. Warman authored the Hateful Posting? The basis for my making
that order was that:

“[114]  In my view, to a large extent in this case the
only relevant information to the plaintiff's libel claim on Mr. Warman's hard
drive would be files which establish whether he was the author of the Hateful
Posting. Mr. Warman has produced an expert report which opines that his computer
was not used to author the Hateful Posting.

[
17
]

That report obtained by Mr. Warman, was
delivered by a company known as “Digital Wyzdom”.

[
18
]

Mr Levant now brings this motion “to enforce the protocol established by the
Order of Master Short” In particular the factum filed
on his behalf asserts that:

“The Plaintiff
has acted contrary to the direction of this Court and has inappropriately redacted information in the report on the
basis of blanket claims of privilege and irrelevancy. The defendant Mr. Levant
has been prevented from meaningfully understanding the contents

of the report.”

IV.       Production of the ICE Report

[
19
]

Steven L. Rogers of Digital Evidence International
Inc. was retained as the ICE to provide a report on the Warman Laptop in
accordance with the Directions and Protocol. Mr. Rogers' report (the "ICE Report")
was dated September 20, 2012. A copy of the ICE Report,
without appendices
,
was delivered to the Defendant on
October 25, 2012
.

[
20
]

Defendant's counsel requested the attachments to the ICE Report. Counsel for the
Plaintiff, insisted that the ICE remove certain privileged documents from the
ICE Report,
at the expense of the Defendant
, prior to agreeing to
provide any of the attachments.
In response Defendant's counsel wrote to request that counsel review the terms
of theProtocol and re-requested
the attachments to the ICE

Report.

[
21
]

Counsel for the defendants, points out that the Protocol does not contemplate the Defendant paying for a privilege review
of the ICE Report. In fact, I note that the document is silent in that regard.

[
22
]

On
July 26, 2013
, the Defendant received
a copy of the ICE Report with heavily redacted appendices.

[
23
]

Seeking an explanation for the redactions,
Defendant's counsel wrote to Mr. Shiller on August 5, 20l3. Mr. Shiller
indicated in a document entitled "Objections to Disclosure" that the
redactions were made on the basis of solicitor-client privilege, litigation privilege
and irrelevancy.

[
24
]

The Defendant’s factum continues:

“10.      The
Plaintiff’s explanations for the
redactions lacked particularity. As such, Defendant's counsel again requested
particulars for the redactions and that Mr. Shiller comply
with the Protocol. Mr. Shiller stated in response, on September 17, 20l3, that due to Mr. Warman’s trial commitments, he would begin the
process of further specifying the reasons for redaction after trial.

11.       On September 30, 2013, Mr.
Shiller provided a revised listing of the basis for  redactions of the appendices to the ICE Report. The list does not
include the nature of the documents.
the date of the documents (although some years are listed) or the
sender/recipients on any correspondence.”

V.        The Search Protocol

[
25
]

To make clear the nature and extent of the
searches undertaken, it is necessary to set out in some detail some of the
components of the directions I provided in 2010 with regard to particular
categories of information:

(A) All
documents and information in electronic form and all computers used by Mr.
Warman at the relevant time

Direction:

Mr. Warman is to confirm in writing
that no other computers were used by him during the time in question for
Internet postings relating in any way to the issues raised in this action. The
Independent Computer Expert ("ICE") shall perform such tests as are
necessary to satisfy the ICE that a proper and true minor-image of Mr. Warman’s
hard drive has been provided.

(B) All documents relating to the
personas Mr. Warman used in posting words on white supremacist or other
racist/hate speech websites, including but not limited to the names "Pogue
Mahone" "Axetogrind", "Lucie", "Mary Dufford",
"Dave McLean" "Gabriel" and "Cynthia".

Direction:

The ICE shall conduct searches for
the following alleged personas and any related metadata concerning these terms
or meaningful fragments of them. found on the hard drive: "Pogue
Mahone" "Axetogrind","Lucie", "Mary
Dufford", "Dave McLean". In addition, the ICE should ensure that
appropriate searches are made with respect to all keywords contained in Table
3, at page 10 of the plaintiff’s expert's report. In all cases, both upper and
lower case forms ought to be searched.

(C) All documents and information
relating to the Lucie postings, including all electronic information:

Direction:

This information is to be sought by
the ICE including the spelling "lucy". As well, the name Aubrack is
to be searched.

(D) All documents and information
showing Mr. Warman's IP address at the relevant times:

Direction:
This information is to be sought by the ICE.

[ ... ]

(N) All documents regarding the
individual "E.L." including those regarding her letter of apology and
its publication online.

Direction:

On consent if any such documents
exist in his possession or control, they are to be produced by Mr. Warman.

VI.       It’s Not There…

[
26
]

The nub of the problem before me is that the ICE
Report confirms what had previously been established from the Digital Wyzdom
reports: that there is
no
evidence on Mr. Warman’s hard drive of the
Hateful Posting, the pseudonym used to make it, or the email address used to
register that pseudonym.

[
27
]

Both reports would seem to establish that no
trace of the Hateful Posting exists anywhere on Mr. Warman’s computer. However
the protocol required searches for the various terms enumerated above and those
yielded numerous “hits”.

[
28
]

I am advised that various Appendices are
attached to the ICE Report.  The Appendices identify 12,000+ pages [sic] of
results from single word searches of Mr. Warman’s hard drive.  Counsel for Mr
Warman states that:

“Like all documentary production, the
Appendices were vetted for relevancy and privilege before being produced to
opposing counsel.”

Mr. Levant is still not satisfied.
He now brings this motion to look behind the redactions for relevancy and
privilege, to obtain the un-redacted Appendices.  Mr. Warman objects to this
motion for four main reasons:

•

Master Short’s Order has been satisfied; or in
the alternative, the spirit and intent of the Order has been satisfied;

•

All relevant documents have been provided as
required by the
Rules of Civil Procedure
;

•

Production of the un-redacted Appendices is not
proportionate and is contrary to the Simplified Rule; and

•

Privilege has been properly claimed and with
sufficient particularity.

VII.      Arguments of Parties

[
29
]

Counsel for Mr Warman opens his argument with a
quotation from paragraph 199 of my original reasons where I reproduced a
portion of a July 27, 2009 article authored by Mr Levant:

“I'm a prospective defendant in a
legal action. That doesn't just give me political and media authority to
criticize them, it gives me tremendous legal tools to go after them, too. I
mean, just stop for a moment to consider all of their internal documents I'll
have access to in discoveries. Media pundits don't have access to hundreds of
internal e-mails or memos. Defendants in defamation lawsuits do. It's going to
be a feast — and it’s all going to be done in the bright lights of a court of
law, and not a kangaroo court of the type preferred by … Warman.”

[
30
]

Mr Warman’s counsel submits that this motion is “nothing other than an attempt by Mr. Levant to derail
the within action, to improperly engage in a fishing expedition, and to prevent
the action from being heard on the merits.” The submissions continue:

This motion also raises a very important question
related to privacy:  Can Mr. Levant have unfettered access to Mr. Warman’s
private information that has nothing to do with the litigation with the pious
hope that some nugget of information will emerge to undermine Mr. Warman in
some way and help Mr. Levant with his stated promise to his readers that he
would feast on Mr. Warman’s internal documents?

[
31
]

In assessing the appropriate approach I have
considered the alleged genesis of the Hateful Posting.
The material filed before me on behalf of Mr. Warman asserts, in part:

“In November of 2003, Mr. Warman
filed a federal human rights complaint against Marc Lemire and Craig Harrison
with regard to material on Mr. Lemire's website that included extensive calls
for genocide.  Permanent cease and desist orders have been ordered against both
men by the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal [“CHRT”].

In the course of the CHRT
proceedings, Mr. Lemire and Mr. Bernard Klatt invented a story that Mr. Warman
authored the Hateful Posting.  Mr. Warman had nothing to do with the Hateful
Posting.

For the allegation that
Mr. Warman had made the Hateful Posting to be true, it relied on the absolute
necessity that Mr. Warman had used the same computer, from the same location,
to make the Hateful Posting and three months later to visit Mr. Lemire’s
website in order to gather evidence for the human rights complaint against him.”

[
32
]

As noted above, to address this, Mr. Warman
retained Digital Wyzdom, an independent firm of computer experts to conduct a
forensic examination of the only computer he used at the time the Hateful
Posting was authored.  Two separate Expert Reports (dated December 17, 2009 and
April 23, 2010) concluded that (i) there was no evidence Mr. Warman’s computer
was even turned on the day the Hateful Posting was authored, and (ii) no evidence
existed of the Hateful Posting anywhere on Mr. Warman’s computer.

[
33
]

The absence of this information on what is sworn
to ne the only personal computer of Mr Warman is obviously significant. However
Mr Levant’s counsel raises the apparent absence of material that one might reasonably
expected to have been found on the hard drive. This relates to the persona
“Dave Mclean”.

VIII.    Dave Maclean Application

[
34
]

In the affidavit material put forward by Mr. Levant,
he maintains that certain search words that should have returned results, did
not.  He cites as an example that Mr. Warman supposedly used the pseudonym
“dave mclean” and that there were no hits for that search.  Mr. Warman asserts
that he did not use the online pseudonym “dave mclean”.  Entry 106 to Mr.
Warman’s supplementary affidavit of documents makes clear that “dave maclean”
was a pseudonym used to write a letter applying for membership in the Canadian
Heritage Aliance”.

[
35
]

The copy of the letter produced by Mr Warman
reads as follows:

“Dear Melissa:

As I mentioned in my email. please
accept this as my membership and I may talk to my housemate to see if he's
interested in joining too although sometimes it's hard to get him interested in
what's going on in the world instead of how the Sens are doing ...

Yours,

[signature “Dave”]

Dave Maclean”

[
36
]

My review of the search terms would seem to make
clear that the string “mclean” was searched and yielded no hits. In my
understanding because the letter  uses the spelling the surname “Maclean” would
not be identified as meeting the defined search criteria. That being the case
and because there is no evidence where the physical letter was originally
created I am not persuaded that the absence of hits on “mclean” raises
sufficient doubt to justify further examination of the hard drive.

[
37
]

Even if I am wrong in this conclusion I am
satisfied that the proper application of proportionality in this case would
support refusing the Order sought by the moving party.

IX.       The Data Array

[
38
]

The Appendices attached to the ICE Report are
12,000+ pages of results from single word searches of Mr. Warman’s hard drive.
Those documents were vetted by his counsel for relevance and privileged, as is
the case with all documentary production.

[
39
]

Counsel for Mr Warman confirmed that in his view
all relevant documentation had been produced in this action.

[
40
]

However, Mr. Levant seeks an Order for detailed
particulars of the information over which privilege and relevance exists. Plaintiff’s
counsel argues that to force Mr. Warman to provide such particulars would cause
immense delay to this action, and great expense to Mr. Warman. The appropriate
resolution of these issues requires a further review of the appropriate
approach to discovery in such cases.

X.        Towards
a More Workable Approach
.

[
41
]

I need to reiterate portions of my initial
decision which was written at the beginning of the implementation of the new
proportionality rule. While some progress has been made,it is clear the bar
still needs to move further towards a proportionally appropriate response in
cases such as this. While the extracts that follow may appear somewhat
disjointed in the quest for a modicum of brevity, I commend the full earlier
text to those with a particular affinity for this developing area of the law. I
have added highlights to particularly helpful portions of the extracts that
follow.

[
42
]

Ontario’s enactment flowed from both British and
American initiatives. I observed:

48
In

Access to Justice
in 1995 Lord Woolf noted in a chapter entitled “The
role of the courts and the parties in the conduct of civil litigation”:

The overall aim of my Inquiry is to
improve access to justice by reducing the inequalities, cost, delay and
complexity of civil litigation and to introduce greater certainty as to
timescales and costs. My specific objectives are:

iii.

to provide
appropriate and proportionate

means of resolving disputes;

iv.

to establish "equality of arms"
between the parties involved in civil cases;

v.

to assist the parties to resolve their disputes
by agreement at the earliest possible date; and

vi.

to ensure that the limited resources
available to the courts can be deployed in the most effective manner for the
benefit of everyone involved in civil litigation.”

[
43
]

In my view, the timescales and the costs,
involved in this case militate for reduction of both items on a go-forward
basis.

[
44
]

"Proportional Discovery: Making It The
Norm, Rather Than The Exception" was the title of an article by Gordon W.
Netzorg & Tobin D. Kern which appeared earlier this year, in Volume 68 of
the
Denver University Law Review
. The extracts that follow, while
omitting the numerous footnotes, nevertheless give a clear exposition of their
view of the problems that have existed with the discovery process.

52
The
situation they describe sounds all too familiar:

Our discovery system is broken. It
is broken because the standard of "broad and liberal discovery," the
hallowed principle that has governed discovery in the U.S. for over seventy
years, has become an invitation to abuse. Only the most well-heeled litigants
can afford to bring or defend a case that is likely to generate significant
discovery, as most cases in this electronic age do. Until the default is
reversed from "all you can eat" discovery to proportional discovery
geared to the needs of the case, as the rules already contemplate, the
courthouse doors will remain closed to legitimate cases that the average
citizen cannot afford to bring or defend.

53
The
article argues the long established "broad and liberal" discovery
long permitted under the U.S. Federal Rules is no longer suited to the current
litigation environment:

"Forty years later, much has
changed. With the emergence of the information society, sentiments among the
bench and bar towards discovery have shifted dramatically. Judges and litigants
now routinely describe modern discovery as a "morass,"
"nightmare" "quagmire," "monstrosity," and
"fiasco." If this is how judges and practitioners describe modern
discovery, imagine the disdain of the parties themselves whose interests the
system is supposed to protect and serve through a "just, speedy, and
inexpensive" resolution of disputes. In 2008, the American College of
Trial Lawyers ("ACTL") Task Force on. Discovery joined with the
Institute for the Advancement of the American Legal System ("IAALS")
to survey members of the ACTL on the role of discovery and any perceived
problems in the United States civil justice system. Nearly 1,500 ACTL members
responded, speaking with an average thirty-eight years of experience in civil
litigation and with nearly equal representation of plaintiffs and defendants.
An overwhelming majority of the survey participants reported that discovery has
become an end in itself -- a costly weapon used to "bludgeon" parties
into settlements. The participants commented that attorneys, rather than
clients, "drive excessive discovery." Forty-five percent of them
believed that discovery is abused in
"almost every case"
and
fifty-three percent believed that changes to the discovery rules since 1976
have
not
curbed the abuse."

54
They
go on to observe:

The Task Force Survey
further revealed a widespread belief that radical changes to the system are
necessary, rather than continued tinkering with the existing rules.
Participants
complained that "[w]e have sacrificed the prospect of attainable justice
for the many in the interest of finding that one needle in the ... haystacks,"
and that "[t]he total lack of control of discovery ... is killing civil
litigation?"
[my emphasis]

…

56
If
the system is broken, the report concludes, then it is time to reverse the
default discovery rule to one of "proportionality". In other words,
it
is time to stop tweaking the rules

and change the default from
"everything is discoverable" to "you only get what you
need." Discovery has become the tail wagging the dog in many (if not most)
civil cases, resulting in "unacceptable delays and prohibitive
expense."

57
Of
particular relevance to this case is their observation:

Judicial attitudes toward the
discovery process and the resolution of discovery disputes show similar
frustration and despair, particularly as electronic information proliferates.
Judges now must moderate and determine a whole host of e-discovery disputes,
including where such information 'resides, in what format, in whose possession,
on what fixed or mobile device, in live, "deleted," or archived
status, on whose server, and on what type of system. And that is just the
start. Judges then must sort through issues such as the existence and relevance
of "metadata," alteration and manipulation of electronic information,
and
the benefits and burdens of allowing or forbidding forensic examinations
….

59
It
is hard to argue with the observation:

"In practice, however, those
protections lie dormant, or are made subservient, to the default rule in favor
of virtually unlimited discovery. Unless and until the responding party can
muster a specific objection to a particular discovery request, with sufficient
evidence to back it up, any and all relevant information must be produced.
The
real burden, in practice, remains upon the party resisting discovery. The bar
is set so high on the resisting party that the default rule in favour of
virtually unlimited discovery of any relevant fact routinely prevails."

61
The
American authors argue:

"The default rule, therefore,
should be reversed: relevant facts should be discoverable
only in proportion
to the specific claims and defenses in dispute,
as determined by the judge
at an early case management conference using factors such as those set forth in
Rule 26(b)(2)(C), and no further discovery of facts should be allowed without a
showing of good cause." Under this reverse default rule, the ability to
show relevancy is not the dominating test; as experience has shown,
"relevancy" is not much of a test at all. Instead, the dominating
factor under the new rule is whether requested discovery passes a threshold,
common sense, cost/benefit analysis under established proportionality factors.

.....

In short, the "strong
preference for broad production" continues to dominate.
So too does the
presumption that the responding party must pay the way of his inquisitive
opponent, whether or not the information sought is in paper or electronic
repositories, live or archived, measured in bankers boxes or in gigabytes.

Conversely, limitations on discovery
are seemed to have been rarely enforced absent a specific, fact-supported
challenge mounted by the resisting party. Courts with crowded dockets seem to
prefer -- or are simply more accustomed to -- resolution of discovery disputes
by an itemized analysis of each disputed discovery request and the sufficiency
of the specific objection.
Still largely missing is any assessment of
whether the discovery sought is proportional in its broader context,
considering the
needs
of the case, the
amount
in controversy, the

significance
of the issues, and the
resources
of the parties
...."
[my emphasis]

[
45
]

I regret that there appears to have been little
change in the approach of counsel over the five year period during which I have
been involved with this case. I reiterate my observation in my previous
reasons, that there needs to be a restraint on the extent of electronic
discovery, so as to continue to endeavour to allow meaningful access to the
courts with a relative equality of arms between litigants. I have seen little
to dissuade me from the beliefs that the following from paragraph 62 of my
reasons still describes the situation for the majority of litigants in this
province:

"Perhaps creation of a
disincentive to sue from the threat of massive discovery is the whole point,
from a defendant's perspective. Intentional or not, massive discovery sends a
message to the next potential plaintiff. And, to be fair, plaintiffs and their
counsel are equally
incentivized by the current discovery system to use the
threat of costly, invasive, and time-consuming discovery to cause defendants to
settle cases quickly for substantial payment rather than pursue valid defenses.
That is not a fair system. That is a system where the party able to launch the
most aggressive and far-reaching discovery campaign prevails, regardless of how
the law applies on the merits."

[
46
]

That is not my vision of a fair, right or just
civil litigation system. I continue to agree with the view of Netzorg and Kern
that the default rule for discovery should start with proportionality, and “a
recognition that
not all conceivably-relevant facts are discoverable
in
every case.” In my earlier reasons I noted the provisions of the US Federal
Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b)(2)(C) , which provided:

On motion or on its
own, the court must limit the frequency or extent of discovery otherwise
allowed by these rules or by local rule if it determines that:

(i)

the discovery sought is
unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, or can be obtained from some other
source that is more convenient, less burdensome, or less expensive;

(ii)

the party seeking
discovery has had ample opportunity to obtain the information by discovery in
the action; or

(iii)

the burden or expense of the proposed
discovery outweighs its likely benefit, considering the needs of the case, the
amount in controversy, the parties' resources, the importance of the issues at
stake in the action, and the importance of the discovery in resolving the
issues.

[
47
]

There continues to be in need to reinforce a
reversal of the previous default rule in favour of proportionality which would
replace relevancy as the most important principle guiding discovery. Relevancy
would remain a threshold requirement,
but would not be a license to obtain
discovery regardless of the burden or expense imposed on the opponent if the
costs of discovery outweigh the likely benefit.

[
48
]

This then brings me to Ontario’s Rule 29.2 headed "
Proportionality in Discovery
" which
makes clear the consistency of approach now in force in both jurisdictions. I
have considered the directions contained in these extracts from the rule:

29.2.02
This Rule applies to any determination by the court ... as to
whether a party or other person must answer a question or produce a document:

29.2.03
(1) In making a determination as to whether a party or other person
must answer a question or produce a document, the court shall consider whether,

a.

the time required for the party or other person
to answer the question or produce the document would be unreasonable;

b.

the expense associated with answering the
question or producing the document would be unjustified;

c.

requiring the party or other person to answer
the question or produce the document would cause him or her undue prejudice;

d.

requiring the party or other person to answer
the question or produce the document would unduly interfere with the orderly
progress of the action
; and

e.

the information or the document is readily
available to the party requesting it from another source.

Overall Volume of Documents

In addition to the considerations
listed in subrule (1), in determining whether to order a party or other person
to produce one or more documents,
the court shall consider whether such an
order would result in an excessive volume of documents required to be produced
by the party or other person.

[
49
]

In hindsight, my approval of the discovery
protocol in this case lead to results which were
against the spirit and intent of the Simplified Procedure Rule, and it could
not have been contemplated by Master Short’s original ruling given the enormity
of the undertaking.

XI.       Other Issues Raised

[
50
]

Counsel for Mr Levant raises a number of issues
with respect to the proposed degree of production by the plaintiff with regard
to the ICE Report. I now turn to the parties’ submissions with respect to those
issues.

(i)          Redactions not
in accordance with Protocol

[
51
]

The ICE Protocol established the terms for the
production of the ICE Report. In particular I provided an opportunity for the Plaintiff
to identify with "full particularity" the information contained in
the ICE Report over which he asserted solicitor-client privilege. Further, the
Plaintiff was required to provide the Defendant with “an appropriately redacted
version of the Report which will have as redactions only that information which
the plaintiff has listed in his Schedule 'B'.”

[
52
]

Counsel for Mr Levant submits that nowhere in
the Protocol does it state that information in the ICE Report ought to be
redacted for relevance. He argues “quite the opposite, only material subject to
solicitor-client privilege was permitted to be redacted under the Protocol.”

[
53
]

While the Protocol was silent on this issue, in
my view the overall thrust of my decision was to narrow the extent of
extraneous production. To allow inspection of irrelevant data was never the
intent of the Protocol and I regard that interpretation as being implicit if
not explicit,
ab initio
.

[
54
]

However, different considerations flow from
items where privilege is asserted as the basis of redaction.

[
55
]

The moving party’s factum asserts that the Plaintiff
has not provided the particulars of the information over which he has asserted
solicitor-client privilege. It is stated that information provided is not
sufficient for the Defendant to meaningfully understand the nature of the
documents or consider challenging the Plaintiffs assertion of solicitor-client
privilege and that this approach is not in keeping with the established
standard for particularization of solicitor-client documents in a Schedule
"B".

[
56
]

The decision of Justice L. B. Roberts in

Shibish v. Honda of Canada lnc.
,
2010 ONSC 3770
, 2010 CarswellOnt 9759 sets out my understanding of
the law in this area:

[10]
It is also well established that parties must list in Schedule "B" of
their affidavits of documents any documents over which they claim privilege,
identify the privilege being claimed for the documents, the persons who are
parties to the communication, including its author, and a description of the
documents sufficient to identify them as relevant to an issue in the
proceeding.

[11] Finally, although production of
a document may be protected by privilege, this does not mean that a party is
excused from disclosing any relevant, factual information contained in
otherwise privileged documents that can be separately gleaned and summarized
from any legal advice or commentary with respect to that information, or that
was obtained by counsel from sources other than the client. Facts that happen
to be reflected in privileged documents are
not privileged from discovery if
had they not been in the privileged documents, they would otherwise have to be
disclosed.
[my emphasis]

[
57
]

Thus privilege need not be asserted if the
information is simply not relevant to the case, as pleaded.

[
58
]

Counsel for Mr. Levant asserts:

16.       The Plaintiff has claimed a
blanket privilege over the redacted material in the ICE Report without
providing adequate information to assess such claims or disclosing the underlying
factual information contained in the documents.

17.       Unlike solicitor-client
privilege, which continues indefinitely if not waived, litigation privilege
only endures until the conclusion of litigation. Litigation privilege creates a
zone of privacy over communications necessary for the parties to prepare their
positions without adversarial intrusions or premature disclosure. Litigation
privilege will "yield more readily to the necessity of the truth seeking
function of the court" than solicitor-client privilege. The Plaintiff has
claimed litigation privilege over a wide swath of material on the basis of
“email headers concerning ongoing litigation (rest irrelevant), emails
concerning ongoing litigation, and misc. related to ongoing litigation.” The
Plaintiff does not identify the proceedings based on which the claims of
litigation privilege are made….”

[
59
]

In determining whether litigation privilege may
continue when two or more proceedings are related, Master MacLeod has observed in
Kaymar Rehabilitation Incorporated v.
Champlain Community Care Access Centre,
2013
CarswellOnt 3530,
2013 ONSC 1754
,
that

[
59]
There is therefore no bright
line test.
It is necessary to analyze the purpose for which the document
was originally created and whether it retains that purpose in the current
litigation. If the document remains necessary to investigation or preparation
in the new litigation and if disclosure would penetrate the zone of privacy
required by the advocates in the litigation it will remain privileged. [my
emphasis]

[
60
]

Here,
counsel for Mr. Levant asserts that:

“It is not
possible for the Defendant to evaluate or challenge such claims if the

[
61
]

In response counsel for the plaintiff asserts:

“The itemization of objections to disclosure provided

]

The affidavit material filed before me, from the

]

It further appears that on September 30, 2013, counsel
for the plaintiff forwarded a revised list of objections to disclosure to

paragraph 4 of his decision, Master Short notes that this litigation centres

to the plaintiff's libel claim on Mr. Warman's hard drive would be files which

[

]

(ii)
The Order has been satisfied; or
alternatively, the spirit and intent of the Order has been satisfied

]

I agree that the purpose of my issuing the ICE
protocol was to have a second opinion on whether or not Mr. Warman could have

[
68
]

The ICE Report confirms what was already known
from the Digital Wyzdom expert forensic reports, that there is no evidence on

[
69
]

In my earlier reasons at paragraphs 25 and 26 I
observed:

As well, the report filed before me of an independent
expert retained on behalf of Mr. Warman reports a determination that "Mr.
Warman's computer was not turned on the date [the Hateful Posting] was
made".

….The filed report includes, at p. 4, a conclusion
that "it is our professional opinion that it would be unsound to reach the
conclusions found in the Klatt affidavit".

[
70
]

While
the ICE Report itself has been fully disclosed to Mr. Levant,
counsel for Mr. Warman has taken the position and submits that the Appendices to the Report do not form part of the Report and its
conclusions. The plaintiff argues that rather, the Appendices are the ICE’s
work product and contain an enormous amount of raw data from Mr. Warman’s hard

[
71
]

It appears that while the original production
order narrowly defined what material from Mr. Warman’s hard drive should be
relevant to these actions, the use of single word search terms, rather than
searching only for multiple consecutive words found in the Hateful Posting,
resulted in Appendices of a huge amount of raw data.  Given the common nature
of the individual word search terms and the relationship of many of them to the
hate propaganda that Mr. Warman has worked against for years, a massive number
of hits are detailed in the Appendices.

[
72
]

Each of the 12,000+ pages had to be individually
reviewed by the Plaintiff and/or his counsel to accurately determine if they

of objections to disclosure contained within these 12,000+ documents.  The

self-evident.

[
73
]

In my view, where the order could not have anticipated the eventual outcome, the spirit of the
Order must be complied with in keeping with common sense and logic, the order Order
in my view was designed to limit the amount of access Mr. Levant had to Mr.
Warman’s hard drive. Handing over 12,000+ pages of raw data from Mr. Warman’s
hard drive, much of which is said to be irrelevant or privileged, is contrary
to the intention of the Order.

[
74
]

This conclusion reflects my interpretation of
the requirements of the rule applicable to this action. The Simplified Procedure Rule was implemented to deal with cost and
delay issues by reducing the number of pretrial procedures in cases involving
smaller amounts of damages.  The Rule acknowledges that there should be some
proportionality between the procedures available to pursue or defend a claim
and the value of the claim.  Rule 76 was designed to foster more cost-efficient
litigation, the faster resolution of disputes and more economical use of
judicial time.

[
75
]

At no time have any of the defendants objected
to this action proceeding under the Simplified Procedure Rules. Disclosure of
the 12,000+ pages of Appendices in un-redacted form is contrary to the
Simplified Rule because it would unduly delay the within action.  It is not the
simplest and most expeditious mode of bringing the within action to trial.

[
76
]

Regrettably this 2008 action has still not
managed to proceed through the examination for discovery stage. I regret
further, that part of that delay flowed from my reserving decisions in these
complex matters.  Regardless of the causes, and delay of this extent is
unconscionable and an end must be put to this so that the matter can finally be
heard on its merits.

[
77
]

It clearly took counsel and Mr. Warman an
enormous amount of time to review the Appendices.  It is reasonable to expect
that if I made the order sought by Mr. Levant, he is counsel and counsel for
other would require a similar amount of time.  I am fully convinced for the
reasons outlined above, that this action should not be interminably delayed
while two or more other sets of counsel review huge swathes of probably
irrelevant documentation.

(iii)       Discovery is
now available to the defendants

[
78
]

One of the primary original justifications
advanced by Mr. Levant for his motion to compel production of the hard drive of

actions brought under Rule 76 (Simplified Procedure) at the time, discoveries
were not permitted.  That fact was one of the justifications for my original

additional factor that results in Mr. Levant’s arguments being given less weight
at this time. As one of the key justifications for his original demand no

(iv)         Have all relevant documents have been
provided as required by the Rules

[
79
]

As discussed above the ICE Protocol does not
discuss redacting the Report for relevancy.  The issue of relevance was not
argued before me on the initial motion, because the parties could not reasonably
have foreseen that 12,000+ pages of data would result from the ICE search.  But
relevance, a central tenet of our disclosure and discovery process, is implicit
in any order with respect to disclosure, because the parties have an obligation
to produce
only
documents that are relevant.  It goes without saying
that irrelevant documentation should not be produced.  Irrelevant documents
have no place in the discovery process.

[
80
]

In my earlier reasons I commented, at
paragraph 43, on the sworn evidence of Mr. Levant at that time: in an argument
placed before me:

I note as well that Mr.
Levant specifically asserts:

30. Contrary to Mr. Warman's
suggestion in paragraph 2, I have no desire to see any records from Mr.
Warman's computer that are unrelated to his lawsuit against me. My interest is
only those records that are relevant to the pleadings [.]

[
81
]

Based on the totality of the evidence presented
before me I am satisfied that Mr. Warman has made
disclosure of all relevant documents pursuant to his obligations under Rule 30
of the
Rules of Civil Procedure
.  Having counsel for the defendants
duplicate these efforts simply does not make sense. In that regard, at
paragraph 130 of my earlier reasons, I observed:

The Court of Appeal explained that the test for
production of the documents in a defamation case, as well as in any other case,
is relevancy. However, the appellate court mentioned that in a defamation case,
where the defendant pleads justification and/or fair comment, the particulars
pleaded will limit the scope of discovery and the inspection of documents. The
court explained that the rationale for this principle was to prevent a person
from defaming another and then obtain access to all his books to see whether
what was said can be justified. A defendant who pleads justification is taken
to be possessed of facts which support the truth of justification [at para.
22]:

As has already been said, the
defendant is only entitled to discovery if he has set out what parts of the
allegedly defamatory statements are facts, the truth of which is relied upon. .
. . This derives from the longstanding policy which discourages persons from
making defamatory statements about others when not possessed of facts which
would support such statements.

[
82
]

My Order was made for a very specific and discrete purpose: To determine whether any

on his computer
to indicate that Mr. Warman authored

XII.     Personal Computers and Privacy

[
83
]

I note as well that my determination with regard
to proportionality has been in part informed by the
fact that information from a personal computer hard drive is at issue. Personal
computers attract heightened privacy interests.  A search of one’s personal
computer is highly invasive.
The Supreme Court of
Canada in
R. v. Vu
,
2013 SCC 60
reaffirmed
the principle expressed in the Court’s prior
decision in
R. v. Morelli,
2010 SCC 8
that
computer searches are among the most invasive of privacy interests and
represent an unprecedented and intrusive invasion of privacy.  To allow Mr.
Levant access to 12,000+ pages of search results from Mr. Warman’s personal
computer, the contents of which have been deemed irrelevant by counsel, would
be a sweeping invasion of Mr. Warman’s privacy and a deterrent to prospective
plaintiffs. As was observed in
the reasons in
Vu
at paragraph
40
::

It
is difficult to imagine a more intrusive invasion of
privacy than the search of a personal or home computer:
Morelli
, at
para.
105
;
R. v. Cole
,

2012 SCC 53
(CanLII)
, 2012 SCC 53,
[2012] 3 S.C.R. 34
, at para.
3
. Computers are “a
multi-faceted instrumentality
without precedent in our society
”: A. D.
Gold, “Applying Section 8 in the Digital World: Seizures and
Searches”, prepared for the 7th Annual Six-Minute Criminal Defence Lawyer (June
9, 2007), at para. 3 (emphasis added). Consider some of the distinctions
between computers and other receptacles.
[Emphasis in original]
